newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST-Italy Feb PPI/WPI y-y gains to mirror Jan.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Italy Feb PPI/WPI y-y gains to mirror Jan.

text.p: Italian producer and wholesale prices are expected to show similar growth year-on-year in February as in January, a Reuter poll of 11 economists showed on Tuesday.
Analysts noted upward pressure on PPI from a rise in non-petroleum raw materials prices and the firming dollar, but the fall in oil prices and continuing weak domestic demand should help offset this.
On average, analysts polled saw PPI rising 0.2 percent monthly and 0.9 percent year-on-year, after 0.3 and 0.9 percent respectively in January.
They saw wholesale prices rising 0.2 percent month-on-month and 1.0 percent yearly, after 0.3 percent and 1.0 percent the previous month.
National statistics body Istat will publish the data at 0700 GMT on Wednesday April 16.

"February PPI data should be positive, despite the fact they will show a rising trend over the rest of 1997," said Paolo Casadio, economist at Credito Italiano in Milan. "Possibile tensions caused by an increase in labour costs will only emerge later in the year," he added.

Rodolfo Dozio, economist at Banca Commerciale Italiana in Milan, noted that according to the employers' federation Confindustria index, non-petroleum raw material prices in February rose 6.4 percent while prices for oil and derivatives fell 6.3 percent.
"But these contrasting trends take effect at different times and in February the rise in non-petroleum prices could prevail and be accentuated by the firmer dollar," Dozio added.
But this did not necessarily mean an automatic rise in the PPI index, analysts said.

"The Istat index is based on output prices. Given the weak internal demand, the higher input prices could result in lower profit margins, without creating tension on output prices," Martino Dolfini, economist at Chase Manhattan in Milan, said.
In the coming months, economists did not rule out a slight increase in prices that could also have an impact on inflation.

"Some slight tension on PPI is possible, but it is not alarming even if it could contribute to a slight rise in inflation," Deutsche Bank said in a note, adding that consumer price inflation could start picking up in the second half of the year after touching a low of 1.7 percent in June.
